newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Chirac reaps fruit of Bolivian soccer campaign.
newsitem.headline: Chirac reaps fruit of Bolivian soccer campaign.

text.p: It was French President Jacques Chirac's highest speech, and former soccer star Michel Platini's highest kick.

At La Paz's packed international stadium, the world's highest at 11,800 feet (3,600 metres), the two partners in soccer diplomacy reaped on Saturday the fruits of a long campaign to keep it a venue for World Cup qualifying games.
"President Chirac, thank you very much. Welcome, Monsieur Platini," the scoreboard proclaimed in French.

The "ola" rolled endlessly around the 50,000-seat Herna Siles Suazo stadium, and the capacity crowd screamed its war chant "Vivivi, vavava, Viva Bo-li-via," as the French and Bolivian under-17 national teams entered the pitch.

Wary of the risk for players from lowlands to perform at such high altitude, the International Football Federation ruled last year Bolivia must play its home games ahead of the 1998 World Cup in France in lower -- and smaller -- stadiums in the towns of Cochabamba or Santa Cruz.
"A great injustice was about to be committed," Chirac told the fans treated to a free-of-charge game to mark his 24-hour state visit.
Before Platini, the chief organiser of the 1998 World Cup, kicked off the game, Chirac explained why he chose to take up a plea from President Gonzalo Sanchez Losada and fight for La Paz.
"You know how much I love soccer and how much I love your country," he said, his voice hardly audible amid the impatient rumour rising from the stadium.
He left for other official duties before the game, cabinet ministers and leading businessmen in his delegation sporting scarves and headbands to the red, yellow and green Bolivian colours.

One of the few world leaders, with King Juan Carlos of Spain, to take the chance of a trip to the high-altitude city, Chirac said La Paz's stadium had hosted World Cup games previously without any incident, including when Bolivia qualified for the Cup finals in 1994.
The French team flew in five days in advance to get accustomed to the low-oxygen atmosphere. As if to prove Chirac's point, they won 2-0.
Chirac said he spared no effort to get his way, lobbying and persuading visiting Latin American heads of state to back him.
"Together, using all our energy, we achieved that your capital and this splendid stadium be able to watch your continent's greatest teams," he said.

His campaign had an obvious diplomatic aim, ahead of his tour of five Latin American nations to revive faded links with the region. Pandering to the subcontinent's love for soccer, he enlisted Platini, a soccer idol in the region since he helped France beat Brazil in 1986.

Despite the advantage of playing in its home high-altitude environment, Bolivia is far from being out of the woods. After half its group's qualifying games have been played, it is trailing Colombia, Paraguay, Argentina and Ecuador.
The first fours qualify for the finals in France.
